investigations.name: discovery-sbml-recovery
investigations.title: Model Recovery from Data — The Recoverability Frontier
investigations.description: The backward direction — recover model structure from data, the inverse of the sibling decomposition investigation. A recovery benchmark: synthetic data from known SBML models across four biological scenarios, with the discovery-engine cycle driving a closed build -> simulate -> compare -> refine loop to rebuild flat SBML — plus a capability ledger that turns each gap into a modular vivarium process.
investigations.question:
Run as a closed build -> simulate -> compare -> refine loop, can the
discovery-engine cycle recover faithful FLAT SBML models from synthetic
time-series targets across a ladder of biological scenarios (mass-action ->
enzyme kinetics -> gene switch -> oscillator), and what modular, vivarium-style
capabilities must be built to close the gaps where it can't?
investigations.hypothesis:
The cycle recovers flat SBML to within trajectory tolerance AND
structural/parameter match for mass-action and Michaelis-Menten out of the box;
nonlinearity (Hill switch) and dynamic structure (oscillator) expose specific
missing capabilities (candidate-reaction proposal, rate-law fitting, structural
scoring, non-recoverability detection), each of which, once built as a modular
process, extends the recoverable frontier. Parsimony separates genuine recovery
from overfitting.

investigations.name: sbml-decomposition
investigations.title: Decomposition Tradeoffs — When to Split an SBML Model
investigations.description: The forward direction — run known SBML models decomposed across coupled process-bigraph engines and measure what each split costs. A head-to-head of ways to run the same model — from a single libroadrunner/CVODE call to a fully hand-written process-bigraph network — plus two boundary probes: scaling a model until Tellurium's build strains, and asking whether an agent-based model can even be an SBML model. Seven member studies, measured on speed × accuracy × composability.
investigations.question: When you have a biochemical model, when should you run it monolithically in Tellurium (libroadrunner/CVODE) and when is it worth decomposing it into vivarium / process-bigraph sub-processes — and what does each point on that spectrum cost in performance and accuracy, buy in composability, and where does Tellurium (and SBML itself) stop being the right tool as models get larger or stop being reaction networks at all?
investigations.hypothesis: Across the spectrum monolithic Tellurium → split → modular → fully-native process-bigraph, performance and accuracy degrade monotonically while composability rises, so no point dominates. Beyond the single-model comparison we predict two boundaries: (a) the monolithic libroadrunner build strains superlinearly as models scale, so decomposition's modularity matters at size even though it is not free on wall-clock; and (b) not every model is expressible as SBML — an agent-based model reduces to an SBML/ODE only in the large-population, well-mixed, deterministic limit.
